Yes. The story uses subtext effectively throughout, which deeply enriches the 1966 suburban Detroit setting rather than feeling forced. 

For example, in the opening scene, Arthur's "jingling his Oldsmobile keys" and worrying about ending up "behind the pillars" has a clear subtext of social anxiety and status-seeking; he isn't worried about missing the religious service, he is worried about not being seen by his peers. Similarly, the descriptions of the physical environment—the "limestone-and-glass edifice," the smell of "Arpege," the "furs and worsteds," and the rows of "Cadillacs and Buicks"—carry the cultural subtext of a post-war Jewish community using material wealth and suburban decorum as a psychological shield against historical trauma. When the ushers fail to stop the gunman because "in a temple, one did not tackle a man in a *yarmulke*," the subtext highlights how their rigid adherence to bourgeois politeness ultimately leaves them vulnerable to the very tragedy they believed their affluence could keep at bay.
